Nestled in the historic heart of Whidbey Island, Crockett Farm exudes rustic charm and timeless elegance. The farm offers breathtaking water views from the ceremony site and expansive territorial vistas that create a stunning backdrop for photographs. Its large reception barn, adorned with original timbers, provides an authentically rustic yet sophisticated setting for a wedding on Whidbey Island. Able to accommodate up to 200 guests, Crockett Farm is an ideal venue for grand celebrations, ensuring a memorable day for all who attend. Wayfarer is a captivating wedding venue steeped in over a century of history. Located in the historic Bayview area of Langley on South Whidbey Island, this enchanting farm hosts elegant weddings for up to 100 guests amidst its open, rolling grounds and lush orchard. The venue features two distinct barns that cater to different aspects of your celebration. The first barn, bright and whitewashed, offers an intimate and serene setting, ideal for a ceremony or smaller reception. ChIJ1a59GXX8j1QRmBF30ebmMkY.about: Kelly moved to Whidbey Island over 18 years ago after spending several years living in Seattle. Seeking a quieter, more simple life, she searched for the right place to call home and found that in a historic 1913 farmhouse set on five acres in beautiful Bayview Valley. After her daughter was born, Kelly wanted a job that allowed her to both be at home and have a fun and creative outlet. With Kelly’s background in marketing and event planning she realized that her farm could be the scene for some amazing weddings. And so, The Wayfarer and Whidbey Island Weddings was born. Kelly began hosting weddings the summer of 2011. Many years and many weddings later, what she and her experienced team love most about their job hasn’t changed. They love to partner with couples to build a wedding that is as beautiful and unique as each couple is. From the quiet early mornings when the team begins setting up, to the ceremony through to dinner, celebratory dancing and the bride & groom’s sendoff, they love to help it all unfold in the way that best reflects each couple. Before opening FLEUR, I spent years in the corporate world while also running a decorating business on weekends — styling small weddings, baby showers, and events, especially during the busy summer seasons. In 2019, I sold all of my rentals, and when the world shut down in 2020, I launched an online floral shop as a creative outlet while still working full-time. Eventually, I took a leap of faith, leaving my job without a set career plan — never imagining that step would plant the seed for what FLEUR would become. Today, FLEUR carries one-of-a-kind, seasonal pieces — guided by our motto, “Unique Flowers for Unique People.” Each design is more than just an arrangement — it’s a personal story, crafted with care and intention. The Sanders and several partners purchased 1,100 acres of land in the Green River Valley west of Kent as an investment. After constructing the Mill Pond and sawmill they began to harvest the timber. As a result, the open fertile farmland allowed for the start of what is now known as the Smith Brothers Dairy Farm. On this land, they founded the standard dairy and mill operations. Between 1908-1910 the Sanders’ mansion was constructed with lumber from the recently invested mill, salvaged glass from the Alaska-Yukon-Pacific Exposition, and excess bricks from the West Valley Highway construction. Most of these original features, which made the Sanders’ Mansion a unique and modern home of the early 1900’s, have been maintained and restored to keep up our Estate as a historical landmark. You can still expect to see original light fixtures in the home and enjoy a warm shower in the very rare and original “cage shower” in the upstairs restroom. ChIJ80raGAV8kFQRuO0OfsS93dw.home: Meadowbrook Farm is 460 acres of scenic and historic public open space in the upper Snoqualmie valley, owned by the cities of Snoqualmie and North Bend. The land is the remaining center of a once vast upper valley prairie, maintained for thousands of years by the Snoqualmie tribe, for plants and hunting. The land was preserved as Open Space in 1996. This website helps you explore Meadowbrook Farm—its history, landscapes, and trails—while offering guidance on how to visit, learn, and care for this shared open space. Meadowbrook Farm is known to the Snoqualmie people as sdukʷalbixʷ baqʷab (Snoqualmie prairie). It is a place of deep cultural significance to the Snoqualmie, who have lived on and cared for this land for thousands of years. By oral tradition, this prairie above Snoqualmie Falls was where Moon the Transformer came to earth and changed the world's plants and animals into the forms we know today. Meadowbrook Farm is home to one of the largest herds of Roosevelt elk in the Snoqualmie Valley. These majestic animals roam freely across the fields and forests, often visible in groups grazing at dawn or dusk. The elk are a year-round presence at the farm and an important part of the valley’s natural heritage, offering visitors a chance to experience wildlife up close while respecting their space. The farm features a network of gentle walking trails that wind through open meadows, wetlands, and forest edges. These paths offer scenic views of Mount Si and the surrounding valley, while providing opportunities to spot elk, birds, and other wildlife. Trails are accessible year-round and are ideal for walking, running, or enjoying a peaceful connection to nature. The farm hosts a variety of community programs throughout the year, from guided nature walks and wildlife talks
ChIJ80raGAV8kFQRuO0OfsS93dw.about: The land that is now Meadowbrook Farm has been a focal point of human activity for at least 13,000 years. In Snoqualmie tribal oral tradition, the origin of both the tribe and the world is tied to this prairie above Snoqualmie Falls, between Mount Si and Rattlesnake Ridge. During the last Ice Age, around 18,000 years ago, massive glaciers advanced and retreated across the region, carving the grooved volcanic bedrock of the Snoqualmie Valley. When a large foothills lake broke through its glacial dam, the valley was flooded and reshaped—leaving behind a broad, flattened landscape of stones, pebbles, and sand. Soon after, the ancestors of today’s Snoqualmie Tribe were living in the valley. For generations, the Snoqualmie people lived on this prairie, hunting elk, deer, and small game, and drying and smoking salmon caught below the falls. Cedar was central to daily life—used for longhouses, canoes, tools, clothing, mats, and baskets. The open prairie provided camas, lilies, bracken fern, wild carrot, and seasonal berries. The prairie itself was carefully stewarded. Every few years, it was intentionally burned to maintain open grasslands for food gathering and hunting. These practices enriched soil nutrients, reduced ecological competition, and supported fire-adapted species such as camas and Garry oak. I spent a lot of time in the flower shop throughout my adolescence, watching and absorbing her unique techniques. Together, we would frequent trips to Dubai and buy silk flowers for the business. All these beautiful memories and experiences is exactly where my admiration for flowers began to bloom. I’d move along to continue my admiration by creating arrangements for loved ones and special occasions in my free time. Fast forward to current day, and with the push of my lovely daughter and daughter-in-law, I recently took a leap of faith and started my very own floral business. I’ve found it extremely fulfilling to honor and carry on the legacy of Fleurette although my mother is no longer with us. I love bringing joy into people’s lives. Joy through flowers.

ChIJERzrnhD3kFQR4DGJZ8pVIVw.home: Farm fresh local flowers grown with love. Hello! We’re Michele and Chantelle the mother-daughter team behind La Flor Farm. The idea for La Flor Farm grew slowly. For many years Michele shared her garden flowers for weddings, tea parties, birthdays, and baby showers. Chantelle’s yard was overflowing with Hydrangeas and Dahlias, she was looking for space to expand her garden. Every Spring and Summer we would collect new Dahlias, Peonies, Hydrangeas, more flower seeds, and nurture them to share with family and friends. It felt scary to dream that we could turn our love of all things flowers into a fully realized dream. Late in the Summer of 2021, we visited a local Dahlia farm, took a million pictures, oohed and aahed, talked the whole way home about what we loved and what we might try if it was our farm. Michele had just ordered a “farm size” order of Roses, Chantelle’s list of Dahlias was insane. It was time. Time to take the leap of faith. Time to give our baby business a name. Time to place all the orders and make connections. There have been so many special people along the way who have been willing to share a part of their garden to grow ours. We’re looking forward to paying that forward as we share our farm flowers with you. We take pride in growing high-quality English garden style, seasonal flowers - harvested at their peak of freshness. As part of the growing slow flower movement. our blooms are hand-snipped at the last possible moment to meet your purchase timing. And because we use appropriate post-harvest care methods that avoid dangerous chemicals, you can breathe deeply and smell our blooms safely. We’re continually adding to our extensive flower collection. From romantic sweet peas and peonies to dahlias and zinnias - our flowers are anything but ordinary!

ChIJD8TNqgsJkFQRFcNVPL3PyKs.home: In 1943, Holly’s grandparents made the heartfelt decision to purchase 40 acres from the Snohomish School District, seeking a fresh start for their family farm. A s Bellevue grew busier and more crowded, the challenges of running a farm in the bustling area became too great. Snohomish, with its open spaces and tranquil charm, called to them as the perfect place to plant new roots. The View was covered with dense woodlands, and for many years, the breathtaking view hidden beyond the forest remained a secret, waiting to be discovered. Over time, this special place became the heart of a family legacy. Here, four generations have grown, sharing love, laughter, and hard work, while 75 years of successful farming flourished, leaving behind a rich story of dedication and togetherness. In January 2016, the family faced the difficult decision to close the farm after years of decline in the farming industry. Though it marked the end of an era, it also opened the door to new opportunities and a chance to reimagine the future. What once was a place of harvest and hard work became a symbol of resilience and the courage to embrace change while honoring a cherished legacy. In January 2019, the Mr. and Mrs. began planning the transformation of the property into a beautiful venue. With structures originally built in the late 1950s that had been abandoned for over a decade, they set out on a journey of reconstruction and renewal, breathing new life into the space. Today, The View spans nearly seven acres of stunning, scenic landscape with breathtaking views. Surrounded by an additional 22 acres, it offers couples endless photo opportunities and the promise of a truly private and unforgettable wedding experience. ChIJIwDpKOsGkVQR5SeZBSzPBts.about: Thornewood Castle has stood for over one hundred years, nestled among old growth fir trees on five acres at American Lake in Washington State. Its fascinating history, however, goes back more than five centuries. This English Tudor/Gothic mansion is one of the few genuine private castles in the United States and the only one on the West Coast. Thornewood Castle was built to the specifications of Mr. Chester Thorne and his wife, Anna. Chester, having been a successful financier and one of the founders of the Port of Tacoma, spared no expense when it came to the planning and construction of this unique country estate for his family. The creation of Thornewood was truly a labor of love. In 1907, Mr. Thorne purchased a 400-year-old Elizabethan manor in England and had parts of it dismantled and shipped piece by piece to be included in the main house. Renowned architect Kirtland Kelsey Cutter was in charge of this most interesting Tudor Gothic project. Thornewood Castle is constructed with concrete and steel on a solid three-foot-thick foundation. ChIJRQVtdPhUkFQRPZ6iPTa_3Y4.home: Celebrating Old Town’s Croatian Heritage Beginning in the 1880’s Croatian immigrants began arriving in Old Town Tacoma. Most of the Croatians who came to Pierce County were from the Adriatic coastline of Croatia, known as the Dalmatian Coast – the islands of Hvar, Vis, Korčula, Brač, and Šolta. They were seafaring people who had left their homeland because of economic and political problems brought on by pressures from Austro-Hungary, then ruled by the Hapsburg regime. Having heard from others who had made their journey to America, many set their sights on making Washington and the shores of Puget Sound – known to resemble their Adriatic homeland – their destination. And with them they brought their trades of boat building and commercial fishing. MORE > When young men first came to Tacoma, it was sometimes predetermined whether he was to call himself Austrian or Slavonian. Some parents wrote ahead to friends in American who operated boarding houses and asked them to look out for their offspring. Mary Barbare Love and Helen Pakasich Kanick wrote, “if the young man came to Sera Kate, who was the widow of George Petrich, he was automatically a Slavonian. If he came to the Boarding house of Sera Perina, who was Mrs. Nick Radonich, he was automatically an Austrian.” The boarding houses usually had a large dining room, kitchen and one bedroom on the first floor. Since there were not enough bedrooms, men slept in tents behind the house. In 1901 the small group of immigrants founded the Slavonian American Benevolent Society (SABS) and the lodge was incorporated on April 10, 1901. SABS quickly became the central social gathering place for food, dancing, singing, companionship and story-telling. Strangers in a new country, the lodge was an essential portal into a new life. Even though 2021 was our first official year as farmers, we hit it hard and carved out a farm field where there had previously just been stinging nettles and blackberry brambles. In just the few short months we had this patch growing more flowers than we could harvest and share! Our goal is to use sustainable, chemical free, and water-wise growing practices. We want to keep our soil, our woods, and our waterways clean and safe for future generations and the creatures that call it home. We want to leave this corner of the world better than we found it. Emily and Paul met in Portland, Oregon — two people with a shared love of wide open spaces, deep roots, and building something meaningful together. When Paul’s family gathered in 2020 hoping someone would step forward to preserve the old church and parson’s cottage on Maxwelton Road, the two of them did not hesitate. This land was not just a business opportunity; it was a homecoming. In 2021, they celebrated their own wedding right here — surrounded by towering Douglas firs, the people they love most, and more than a century of family history — and Cascadia Meadows was born. The Little Brown Church has anchored the Maxwelton Valley since 1908, when Paul’s great-great-grandparents John and Sarah Grubb arrived from Kansas and, along with Paul’s great-grandparents George and Effie Grubb, founded a Free Methodist congregation on the corner of French and Maxwelton roads. The chapel they built from locally milled cedar weathered to a warm, distinctive brown over the years and became a beloved landmark for generations of South Whidbey families — the fifth generation of Grubbs among them. ChIJa1EmC-iumlQRywiXlm2Sml4.home: Green Gates is a unique five acre wedding and events venue located on beautiful Flowing Lake in scenic Snohomish, Washington. The setting provides a romantic and serene experience with the perfect blend of rustic elegance. The attention to detail in the meticulously maintained gardens as well as the "salvaged and re-purposed" style in all the structures will leave guests awestruck. Stunning photo opportunities are seemingly endless - from the lake, to the grapevines, to the woods, to the rose garden gazebo, to the authentic log cabin...it's a photographer's delight! The comfort provided by the spacious Bridal Cottage and the historic Groom's Cabin will make the day complete. Green Gates can accommodate up to 175 guests mid-May through September only. In appreciation and support of our military and law enforcement, we offer a discount to active duty personnel. Please email us to schedule your personal tour. We look forward to meeting you!
ChIJa1EmC-iumlQRywiXlm2Sml4.about: Green Gates is located on Flowing Lake near the historic town of Snohomish, Washington. Flowing Lake has a rich history going back to the early logging days when logs were floated across the lake to the mill on nearby Panther Lake. In those days, wooden row boats were available for rent at the Wonderland Park Resort for $2.00 per day. Although those days have long since passed, Green Gates is proud to be a part of preserving that rich history. Several of the original Wonderland Park wooden row boats have been salvaged and are now on display at Green Gates. The property that would eventually become Green Gates at Flowing Lake was once a modest equestrian estate. The original 3-horse barn has been beautifully transformed into the Bridal Cottage, and the former covered riding arena in the large barn is now the ballroom reception area. The wedding lawn has a sweeping view of the sparkling lake, lush greenery, and Cascade mountains. The owners of Green Gates acquired the property after falling in love with the barns and the lake, with no real aspirations of becoming a wedding venue. When their daughter’s best friend asked them to host her wedding, they gladly agreed. The rest, as they say, is history.

Song River is an indoor venue that exudes class and elegance for wedding ceremonies and receptions but is simultaneously versatile to incorporate your own vision Located in historic downtown Monroe, a mere 30 miles northeast of Seattle, our venue is nestled within walking distance of the picturesque Skykomish River. Experience the perfect blend of beauty, elegance, and charm at Song River Banquet & Event Center. Come and let us make your dreams a reality. ChIJczP8VmSnmlQRtpz9g1ClaV4.about: Song River started as a vision of owner Quyen Huynh, who saw a way to transform this beautiful space and bring more vibrancy to the community of downtown Monroe. With the hope to build on and build up other women entrepreneurs, Quyen works with exceptional women to create a foundation for Song River. Song River was once known as The Eagles Club for many decades, a watering hole for all Monrovians to gather and celebrate. Almost everyone who grew up in Monroe has spent time here with family and friends. Between 2008 through 2017, this building took on identities of a steak house, a BBQ joint, and a fine dining restaurant. Over the years, the space morphed and transformed with each different tenant. Finally in 2018, the owner decided that it is time to give this uniquely large and beautiful space an opportunity to shine. With 16,000 square feet of space, original hardwood floors, two commercial kitchens and being in Historic Downtown, Song River received a complete make-over, and opened its doors in November 2018. ChIJk95-HYeqmlQRbVvK6q5lf0M.about: Wholesale Flowers by Cascade Floral: After 15 years as managers of a Safeway store in Tacoma, Dorrie, 32, and Elaine, 28, Ransick moved to Everett in 1947 and purchased an existing grocery store located on Broadway. They renamed the store Stadium Market because of its proximity to the Everett Memorial Stadium. Everyone told them they were crazy because the location was too far south of downtown but, from the beginning, they had a thriving grocery business. In 1960, Safeway built a supermarket store a half block away, severely impacting their small grocery business. Elaine decided that in order to survive, they needed to branch out. She had always loved flowers and supposed that, like groceries, if the price was lowered, the demand would increase. Her theory proved right and Elaine offered Easter lilies for her first floral venture. Eventually, she began to carry cut flowers by her customers’ request and then innovated a way to sell flowers to a mass market by selling loose bunches in buckets. By 1971, they had a full-time designer and a delivery truck. In 1972, Dorrie passed away at the age of 57 leaving Elaine with the responsibility of the business. Cheryl, her daughter, and Spark Van Winkle, her son-in-law, came to work to help Elaine. They remodeled and updated the Broadway store. ChIJm4FQEdIGkVQRogkPhrFjLV4.about: The Discovery and Development of Lakewold Emma transferred her lakeside property to her son, Hubbard Foster (H.F.) Alexander, and his wife, Ruth, in 1918. A shipping magnate, H.F. was president of Admiral Lines, one of America's largest passenger steamship companies. He and Ruth had a home in Tacoma at 5th and Yakima and used the house at Gravelly Lake as a country retreat. The Alexanders bought an adjoining 5-acre lot, creating the 10 acres that Lakewold enjoys today, and hired designers to lay out the home and gardens to capture views of Gravelly Lake and Mount Rainier. Ruth named the estate "Inglewood," and the family entertained at the lakeside estate with lawn parties and family weddings. An active garden club member in Tacoma, Ruth had a rose named for her, the climbing "Ruth Alexander." In 1908, Emma Alexander knew a good piece of property when she saw it. Streetcars provided easier access to the Lakes District, and when Interlaaken was platted, Emma bought Lot 23 and built a small summer cabin on the property between 1910 and 1912. By 1913, the gardens were already locally famous, as the Tacoma Daily Register headlined "Nature-loving Tacomans Make Modern Arcady of Gravelly Lake's Shores" (11/30/1913). In 1925, Major Everett Griggs and his wife, Grace, purchased the property and renamed it "Lakewold," a Middle English term meaning "lake-woods." The Making of a Horticultu

Viewing is best done March through May. From the beautiful peeling bark of the Paper Bark Maple, Acer grisium, to their unrivalled fall color, the Japanese maple has become a quintessential northwest garden plant. Lakewold has 30 Japanese maples to view, including two state champions, but it’s our prized beauty Acer ‘Shindeshojo’ that gets all the attention. ChIJsYUDiexbhVQRlY0PVBOjlKg.about: Built in 1912, Restored in 1992, Loving Cared for 36 years, & Currently standing for 114 years on Florence Island Snohomish County Pioneer John P. Anderson made the perilous trek to the Klondike during the gold rush of 1897-1898 in the Yukon. He made claim 42 on Bonanza creek home over that small stretch of years and would continue to visit and work the claim well into the early 20th century. In 1912, J.P. returned home to Washington and settled on 210 acres two miles south of the town of Stanwood in the tiny town of Florence on Florence Island in the Stillaguamish River Valley and built what we now call The Lady Florence. The J.P. Anderson family farmed the ground and resided in the home until the 1950’s when the property was placed in trust of the local lawyer and consequently rented out to many different people during the 60’s, 70;s and 80’s. In 1990 local longtime seed farmer Mark Christianson and his wife Elizabeth purchased the property from the original Anderson family and completely refurbished the home inside and out. The roof was leaking from the 3rd floor to the first floor, all the plaster was removed and all systems of power, heat, security, insulation and drywall were replaced. A couple of camera upgrades later (oh... and the birth of my second daughter, Gabriella, in 2007 and my son, Mason, in 2011), with the encouragement of my wife, Michelle, I decided to start studying the art of portraiture and taking a stab at professional photography. Dabbled in family portraits… tried my hand at weddings/events… even did a little product photography over the past decade. Through all of that, I found myself happiest when I was one-on-one with a face in front of me, working with them to create a headshot for whatever their need was. ChIJyYkHorlvkFQRwBx-Srip2i8.about: In 1926, a group of Swedish immigrants living in Ballard were looking for a farm to buy to build a retirement home, learn English, and get together with fellow countrymen. They found a 36 acre farm with about 1,300 feet of waterfront on Lake Sammamish that even came with a one-eyed horse! The beauty of the farm in its idyllic setting was eventually purchased for $25 and became Vasa Park Resort. In 1945, following the invention of social security, members decided to convert the park into a non-profit and open the gates to the public. In 1929 the Event Center was built to be a dance hall for the local Swedish community. In the early 1950s the Vasa Park Resort Event Center was transformed into a popular roller rink. The popularity of the space attracted alternate opportunities like becoming a concert venue used by promoter Pat O'Day. Throughout the 1960s the space hosted concerts for Conway Twitty, Ray Charles Band with Dave Lewis Combo, and Thomas and His Tomcats featuring a teenaged guitarist named Jimi Hendrix. Vasa Park Resort remains one of the oldest private parks anywhere in the metropolitan area and has been updated to host corporate events, galas, weddings, and more!
